title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: PLAC dying-you-die ≠ privation of justice; Christ blocks
pass_a_gloss: Placeus has already proved dying you shall die is not death as privation of justice—absurd for a law to threaten loss of justice, or a judge to strip justice from those he judges. God did not fulfill that legal threat in Adam, because of Christ's future satisfaction. If the words meant bodily and eternal death, punishing and not punishing, imputing and not imputing, justifying the guilty yet fulfilling the threat cannot stand together. So Placeus will not believe God stripped Adam of original justice and made the just man unjust.
pass_b_english: PLAC. I argued, I say—I have already proved that by the words dying you shall die is not to be understood a death seated in the privation of justice. For what is more absurd than either that a law should threaten the privation of justice, or that a judge should strip of justice those whom he judges? I have also proved that God did not fulfill that threat of the law in Adam, on account of Christ's future satisfaction. And how could it have been fulfilled, if by those words death of body and eternal death were signified? To punish according to the law's threat and not to punish; to impute sin and not to impute; to justify the guilty and yet in him fulfill the law's threat—if I understand anything—so fight that they cannot stand together. Far be it therefore that I believe God stripped Adam of original justice and made him from just into unjust.
source_text: PLAC. Argui, inquam, iam probavi verbis morte morieris non esse intelligendam mortem sitam in privatione justitiae. Quid enim absurdius, quam, aut legem comminari privationem justitiae, aut judicem spoliare eos quos judicat justitia? Probavi etiam Deum illam comminationem legis non adimplevisse in Adamo, ob futuram Christi satisfactionem. Et quomodo potuit adimpleri, si verbis illis mors significabatur corporis & aeterna? punire secundum legis comminationem & non punire: peccatum imputare & non imputare: justificare reum & tamen in eo adimplere legis comminationem, si quid intelligo, ita pugnant, ut consistere simul nequeant. Absit igitur ut credam Deum spoliavisse Adamum justitia originali, ac eum ex justo fecisse injustum.
